paper: OSTI 2448207 — Fierro et al., Massively parallel axisymmetric fluid model for streamer discharges (Comput. Phys. Commun. 2024, DOI 10.1016/j.cpc.2024.109345)

questions.q: Does the paper's observed first-order spatial convergence survive the fully coupled nonlinear r–z axisymmetric streamer problem, or does the semi-implicit n↔φ↔E sub-iteration (2–5 cycles) degrade the effective order below 1 near the moving ionization front?
questions.basis: The MMS confirmation reported here (observed order p=0.995 in L∞) was done on a linear, periodic, 1-D surrogate with fixed v and D. Fig. 7 of the paper measures error on the fully coupled streamer with a self-consistent Poisson solve and a stiff local-field ionization source. First-order stencils can lose an effective half-order at unresolved fronts, and the 2–5 sub-iterations may not fully converge the nonlinear coupling at every step. The replication's MMS check is necessary but not sufficient evidence for the paper's coupled-order claim.
next_steps: Extend the MMS to a 2-D r-z axisymmetric geometry with the paper's geometric source terms (1/r Jacobian) to isolate any order loss from the axisymmetric flux integration.
Add a manufactured local-field-like source Q_src(n_e, E) and iterate the n↔φ↔E coupling with the paper's stated 2–5 sub-iterations; measure observed order as sub-iteration count varies from 1 to 10.
If feasible on a small HPC allocation, rerun Fig. 7 at the reported Δh sequence with the released code and compare per-Δh peak-E error against the paper's plot.

questions.q: Is the paper's <1% peak-E convergence at Δh≈4 μm (C6) a property of the streamer physics itself (front width sets the resolution requirement) or of a fortunate cancellation between upwind numerical diffusion and the physical drift-diffusion, which would fail for different reduced electric fields E/N or gas mixtures?
questions.basis: 1st-order upwind advection is well known to add O(Δh·|v|) numerical diffusion. For a streamer front of physical width w, the effective front will be resolved to O(max(w, Δh)). At Δh≈4 μm and typical air streamer front widths of a few tens of μm, numerical diffusion can smear the front by a comparable amount to the physical diffusion. The 1% peak-E convergence may hold specifically for the CWI benchmark parameters but not generalize.
next_steps: Repeat the paper's Δh sweep at reduced field E/N values that produce narrower fronts (higher pd) and check whether the 1% peak-E convergence still holds at 4 μm or whether the required Δh shrinks proportionally.

Repeat with a Koren-limited advection variant (the paper's alternative) at the same Δh and compare peak-E convergence rates; if Koren converges faster in Δh, the 1st-order convergence is genuinely limited by upwind numerical diffusion, not by physics.

Instrument the front-width diagnostic (FWHM of n_e near the tip) at each Δh; if front width plateaus at ~Δh rather than at a physical value, the paper's convergence claim is resolution-limited, not physics-limited.

questions.q: How large is the streamer-velocity overestimate from 1st-order upwind (paper's C8) relative to Koren flux-limited under a fair, stable comparison, and does it scale linearly with Δh as the discretization theory would predict?
questions.basis: The paper asserts (Fig. 10) that 1st-order upwind overestimates streamer velocity compared to a Koren flux-limited scheme. The replication attempted a 1-D nonlinear surrogate but hit forward-Euler explicit-source blow-up at fine Δh, so this claim is entirely unverified externally. The magnitude and Δh-scaling of the overestimate matter because they set the physical-fidelity gap between the paper's production runs and higher-order alternatives (e.g., MUSCL, DG).
next_steps: Rebuild the 1-D nonlinear surrogate with a semi-implicit source treatment (implicit ionization) or RK-IMEX time stepping to suppress the explicit-source blow-up that made the current surrogate unstable at fine Δh.
At matched Δh, run upwind vs. Koren and record streamer-tip velocity vs. time; fit velocity-overestimate as a function of Δh to check linearity.
Compare against a published higher-order streamer code (e.g., Afivo or Cerrone-Popov) as an external anchor if a lightweight benchmark script is available.

questions.q: At what processor count does the MueLu-preconditioned GMRES Poisson solve become the true wall-clock bottleneck (paper says ≥512), and is that crossover mesh-size-independent (weak scaling) or a fixed-work strong-scaling artifact?
questions.basis: The paper reports near-perfect strong scaling of the FV kernel up to 256 procs (2× procs → 2× speedup) and FV scaling to 1024, with the field solver as the bottleneck at ≥512. The replication did not rerun on a cluster (C9 out of scope). Whether the field-solver bottleneck reflects an intrinsic AMG-communication scaling wall or a fixed problem-size effect is important for anyone porting the code to larger allocations.
next_steps: Run a matched weak-scaling study (constant elements per proc) from 64 to 2048 procs using the paper's Trilinos/Belos+MueLu setup on a comparable machine (e.g., Polaris) and record the FV-vs-Poisson time fraction at each proc count.
Vary the MueLu coarsening rate and smoother sweeps to test whether the ≥512-proc bottleneck can be pushed higher with tuning, or whether it is fundamental to the current AMG choice.
Compare against an alternative preconditioner (e.g., BoomerAMG from Hypre, or FFT-based Poisson on the axisymmetric mesh) at 512–2048 procs to characterize the AMG-specific cost.

questions.q: How sensitive is the CWI-benchmark agreement (paper's peak-E within 5%) to the tabulated transport-and-rate coefficients (μ_e, D_e, ᾱ)? Would using a different community table (Bolsig+ vs. LXCat vs. LoKI) shift peak-E enough to change the paper's ‘within 5%’ conclusion?
questions.basis: In fluid streamer models the local-field-approximation Q_src = ᾱ μ_e |E| n_e depends on tabulated coefficients whose values can vary by several percent across community sources for the same reduced field E/N in the same gas. A 5% peak-E agreement is close to the between-table spread. The replication did not have access to the specific tables used by the paper, so cannot separate ‘code+method agreement’ from ‘table agreement’.
next_steps: Confirm exactly which transport/rate table version and cross-section source the paper used (Bolsig+ solver version, LXCat database snapshot date) and archive it with the replication artifacts.
Rerun the benchmark case with two alternate widely-used tables (e.g., Bolsig+ with Phelps vs. Biagi cross sections) and quantify the peak-E spread at the same times as Fig. of the CWI comparison.
If the spread ≥5%, downgrade the paper's ‘within 5% of CWI’ claim to a statement conditional on the specific table used, and recommend the community benchmark itself pin the table.
